evidence_cards.title: MEPS 2016: people with a reported ICD-10 A69 (other spirochetal infections, which includes Lyme disease)
evidence_cards.definition: People with at least one condition record whose 3-character ICD10CDX equals A69.
evidence_cards.method: Sum of unique-person weights (PERWT16F) over the domain; standard error by Taylor linearisation over VARSTR/VARPSU. Person-level, one year only.
comparability: A69 is the broad category that contains Lyme (A69.2x); MEPS public files keep only the first 3 characters, so this is NOT a Lyme-specific count and must not be read as Lyme prevalence.
MEPS panels overlap across adjacent years: never add or pool these yearly totals.
Condition rows come from household reports coded by professional coders.

AHRQ (MEPS team, 2026-09-24) urges caution forming Lyme cost estimates from MEPS: pooling 2016-2024 gives only about 300-400 observations, expenditures are highly skewed (about 1,000 or more are needed for a solid mean), only treated Lyme is identified (zero-expenditure cases drop out, biasing upward), events may be flagged as arthritis without naming Lyme, comorbidities cannot be separated from Lyme, and onset dates are not recorded. Lyme-specific A69.2 is available only in restricted data centers.

uncertainty.note: Small samples give very wide, unreliable intervals.

evidence_cards.summary: 2016: about 436,208 people (95% CI 250,739 to 621,678; 31 sampled persons) reported a condition coded A69.
evidence_cards.how_to_use: Cross-check or population context only, never a prevalence of Lyme or Long COVID; not a cost estimate (events are counts, not dollars).

evidence_cards.method: Weighted mean (ESAQ person weight ESAQWT24F) with a Taylor-linearised standard error from VARSTR and VARPSU; adults who skipped an item are excluded from that item.
evidence_cards.source_locator: MEPS HC-256 (2024 Full-Year Consolidated): EQMVAM53, EQOVAM53, EQMBAM53, EQPPAM53, EQCARE53, ESAQWT24F
comparability: All U.S. adults who answered the questionnaire, not people with Lyme disease or Long COVID: MEPS cannot identify either condition reliably (AHRQ, 2026-09-24).
Fielded in 2024 only: the questionnaire was funded for that year, so there is no trend and no later update.

Self-reported. MEPS top-coded the annual hours at the 99.5th percentile (Table 13 of the HC-256 documentation: 2,080 hours for own visits, 1,040 for others' visits, 720 for bills, 520 for paperwork), so a few very large values are capped. About 6% of respondents skipped each time item, and MEPS notes that about 20% of those who completed the paper version gave no answer to them.
Hours, not dollars. Converting hours to dollars needs a published wage or value-of-time source shown next to the estimate.

scientific_analysis.plain_language_summary: This is a 10th-anniversary chartbook from LymeDisease.org summarizing findings from MyLymeData, a patient-powered registry of over 19,000 U.S. Lyme disease patients. It reports high rates of diagnostic delay and misdiagnosis, heavy co-infection burden, worse quality of life and higher healthcare utilization among patients with persistent Lyme disease (PLD) compared to acute Lyme disease patients and the general population, and describes substantial barriers to care including insurance non-acceptance, travel distance, and clinician scarcity. It also reports work-schedule disruption (reduced hours or quitting work) among a large share of PLD patients and cites one external claims-based estimate that Lyme disease costs the U.S. healthcare system about $1 billion a year. Most figures come from self-reported registry survey data, with several key background statistics drawn from previously published external studies rather than measured directly by MyLymeData itself.

The 'Lyme Infection Associated Chronic Illness (Lyme IACI)' umbrella concept is mentioned as including chronic fatigue syndrome and Long COVID, but no Long COVID-specific data, burden, or cost figures are reported anywhere in this document.
evidence_gaps: No direct-medical-cost dollar figures (e.g., total or per-patient annual spending) are reported by MyLymeData itself; the only dollar figure ($1B/year) is an external, claims-based citation with no stated price year or converted per-patient cost.
No direct non-medical cost dollar amounts (e.g., dollar cost of travel, paid help, home modification) are given; only travel-distance percentages and special-equipment-use percentages are reported.

No indirect-cost dollar amounts (lost wages, lost income) are reported; only percentages of patients who reduced hours or quit work are given, with no wage or income data to convert this into a lost-income estimate.
No lifetime or multi-year cumulative cost projection is offered; quality-of-life and health-status data are reported longitudinally (6 months to 5+ years) but not linked to any cost trajectory.

No disaggregation of any modeled cost, utilization, or access-barrier figure by age, race/ethnicity, disability status, sexual orientation, gender identity, veteran status, or marital/familial status is reported; only a sex-based sub-study (Johnson et al. 2023) provides any subgroup breakdown.

The claims-based $1 billion/year Adrion et al. 2015 estimate would need a stated price year and a reconciliation with self-reported utilization multipliers before it could be used to build a per-patient direct-cost model.
comparison_boundaries: Do not pool the CDC's cited ~500,000 annual Lyme disease case estimate (national, year unspecified) with the DeLong et al. 2019 cumulative estimate of ~2 million Americans with persistent Lyme disease (PLD): one is an annual incidence estimate, the other a cumulative prevalence estimate over an unspecified/different time frame, from different sources.

Do not pool the two different general-population comparator percentages for 'fair/poor health status' cited in this document: 13% (DeLong 2019, page 8) and 16% (Johnson et al. 2014 quality-of-life survey, page 20-21) - these come from different studies/samples and should not be treated as a single general-population baseline.

Do not pool the self-reported MEPS-style healthcare utilization figures collected directly through the MyLymeData registry (page 23) with the Adrion et al. 2015 insurance-claims-based $1 billion/year cost estimate: different data sources (patient self-report vs. insurance claims), different populations (self-selected registry enrollees vs. >50,000 claims-identified patients), and no shared or stated price year.

The MyLymeData registry population (self-selected, 85% women, weighted toward patients with persistent/chronic symptoms) should not be treated as representative of the general U.S. Lyme disease population or of CDC surveillance case counts; percentages reported here describe the registry sample, not a population-representative rate.

The research term 'Post-Treatment Lyme Disease' (PTLD), which after RCT exclusion criteria represents roughly 10% of those seeking to enroll, is a much narrower and more restrictive population than 'persistent Lyme disease' (PLD) as MyLymeData defines it (clinically diagnosed, ill ≥6 months after antibiotic treatment); do not conflate PTLD study findings with PLD registry findings.

The two slightly different lab-test-support percentages for PLD diagnosis (78% on page 7 vs. 85% on page 13) come from different figures/framings in the chartbook and should not be silently merged into one number.

sex_gender_findings.finding: A 2023 MyLymeData sub-study (Johnson et al. 2023, University of Washington collaboration, >2,000 PLD patients) found that women reported more tick-borne co-infections, longer diagnostic delays, greater symptom severity, and worse functional impairment than men, and were more likely to be misdiagnosed (particularly with chronic fatigue syndrome, fibromyalgia, or psychiatric disorders); no differences were reported between men and women in antibiotic treatment response or side effects. Separately, 85% of overall MyLymeData registry participants are women.

claims_undercounting_caveat.basis: The chartbook directly quotes Adrion et al. (2015), describing it as 'a big data study out of Johns Hopkins using insurance claims records of over 50,000 Lyme patients' that found the $1 billion/year healthcare system cost figure; this is explicitly an insurance-claims-based source, which the chartbook itself elsewhere notes captures only insured services and would miss the roughly half of PLD patients whose treating providers do not accept insurance.

subgroup_disaggregation_caveat.pooled_value: The PLD healthcare utilization figures on page 23 (annual doctor's visits of 19.4 vs. 1.09, ER visits of 3.7 vs. 0.43, hospital inpatient stays of 15% vs. 13%, and home care visits of 8% vs. 2%, comparing PLD patients to the general population) are presented as single pooled national figures with no breakdown by sex, age, race/ethnicity, disability status, sexual orientation, gender identity, veteran status, or marital/familial status, and the document does not state that subgroup variation in these utilization rates was checked.

systemic_gap_caveat.description: The chartbook describes a combined clinician-training/access gap and a research gap: it states that 'despite the growing number of [PLD] cases, very little research has been conducted on how best to treat them,' and separately describes a supply-and-demand imbalance in which most clinicians who treat PLD do not participate in insurance networks or Medicare/Medicaid, face prior-authorization and insurance-denial burdens, and report being stigmatized by colleagues or reported to medical boards for treating PLD.
systemic_gap_caveat.basis: Overview section (page 7: 'Despite the growing number of these cases, very little research has been conducted on how best to treat them') and Clinician Barriers to Providing Care section (page 19: ~75% of clinicians do not participate in insurance networks, ~77% do not participate in Medicare/Medicaid, 39% report being reported to a medical board/insurer/quality-improvement inquiry, and 75% report feeling stigmatized or disrespected by colleagues for treating Lyme disease).

decision_relevance.summary: Patients and advocates could use a simulator built from this document to understand typical diagnostic-delay pathways, symptom burden, and the access-to-care and insurance barriers reported by a large real-world PLD patient population, helping frame conversations with clinicians or insurers about treatment history. Care delivery teams could use the reported healthcare-utilization multipliers (e.g., roughly 5x more doctor visits, roughly 2x more ER visits than the general population, self-reported) to anticipate the intensity of care PLD patients require when planning clinic capacity. Payers and policy audiences could use the reported insurance-access statistics (e.g., ~75% of PLD-treating clinicians outside insurance networks, ~50% of patients whose provider doesn't accept insurance, 27% unable to find a treating clinician) to evaluate network-adequacy and access gaps, while recognizing that this document supports none of these uses with an independently modeled total or per-patient direct-cost figure - only one externally cited, claims-based $1 billion/year system-cost estimate with no stated price year.
use_cases: Care-access barrier explorer: let users see how insurance non-acceptance (50% of providers), inability to find a treating clinician (27%), and travel distance (32% traveling 100+ miles) combine to delay or prevent PLD treatment, without implying these percentages generalize beyond the MyLymeData registry sample.

Healthcare-utilization-intensity comparator: let care delivery planners compare self-reported PLD utilization rates (doctor visits, ER visits, hospital stays, home care visits) against the general-population baseline reported in this document, clearly labeled as self-reported registry data, not claims-derived.

Cohort/subgroup design screening aid: given the document's extensive discussion of clinical-trial exclusion criteria (RCTs excluding 89-99% of real-world PLD patients) and treatment-response heterogeneity (High/Low/Non-Responders), a simulator could flag the value of screening trial cohorts for unmeasured confounders - such as home environmental exposure (mold, mildew, pet dander) - before attributing response variance to a studied treatment, since this document already shows unexplained subgroup variation in treatment response that averages can obscure.

spec.title: Persistent Lyme Disease: Diagnostic Delay, Access Barriers, and Care Utilization (MyLymeData 2025 Chartbook)
spec.boundary: This simulation reflects self-reported findings from the MyLymeData patient registry (19,000+ enrollees, 85% women) as summarized in LymeDisease.org's 2025 chartbook, focused on the subset of participants who report persistent Lyme disease (PLD). It covers diagnostic delay, misdiagnosis, insurance/clinician access barriers, and self-reported healthcare utilization, plus one externally cited insurance-claims-based system cost estimate. It does not include any MyLymeData-generated dollar cost figure, any nationally representative incidence/prevalence estimate, caregiving burden, or a lifetime cost projection - none of these are reported in the source document. The registry sample is self-selected and skews toward more severe, persistent illness, so percentages here describe this sample, not the general U.S. Lyme disease population.

takeaway.patient: In this patient-registry sample, most people who went on to have persistent Lyme disease were not diagnosed quickly: about three-quarters were still undiagnosed at six months or more, and about three-quarters were given a different diagnosis first. Half of respondents say their treating provider does not accept insurance, and people with persistent Lyme disease in this sample reported seeing a doctor far more often per year than the general population comparator. These are patterns reported by a self-selected group of patients with ongoing symptoms, not a guarantee of any one person's path.
takeaway.care: This registry data suggests a workflow pattern worth noting: a majority of persistent Lyme disease patients in this sample were initially diagnosed with something else before Lyme was identified, and most were not diagnosed until the illness was already prolonged. Combined with a far higher reported visit frequency than the general-population comparator and a reported pattern of limited insurance-network participation among treating clinicians, this points to care that is intensive, often delayed, and frequently delivered outside standard insurance-based workflows - relevant to intake protocols, referral pathways, and capacity planning.
takeaway.policy: Among this self-selected registry sample, diagnostic delay and misdiagnosis before a persistent Lyme disease diagnosis are common, half of patients report their provider does not accept insurance, and self-reported utilization (doctor visits per year) is sharply higher than the general-population comparator. patient: If your own diagnosis took longer than expected, this data shows that's a common pattern in this patient group, not a sign something is unusual about your case specifically.

Consider connecting with a patient advocacy organization (such as the one that runs this registry) for guidance navigating insurance and access barriers, since these barriers are widely reported in this sample.
care: This registry's finding that most persistent Lyme disease patients were first diagnosed with something else may be worth checking against your own intake and differential-diagnosis workflow for patients presenting with chronic fatigue, fibromyalgia-type, or psychiatric symptom pictures.

package.documentation:
## Source
All figures come from LymeDisease.org's MyLymeData 2025 Research Chartbook, a 10th-anniversary summary of a patient-powered registry of 19,000+ U.S. Lyme disease patients (85% women), focused on the subset self-reporting persistent Lyme disease (PLD) - defined as remaining ill ≥6 months after antibiotic treatment.

## What the inputs represent
- Diagnostic delay (77% diagnosed at ≥6 months) and misdiagnosis (74% initially given a different diagnosis) are self-reported, distinct measures: one is about timing, the other about diagnostic accuracy before correction.
- Insurance non-acceptance (50% of providers) and the doctor-visit utilization comparator (19.4 vs. 1.09 visits/year) are both self-reported registry figures, not claims data.
- The $1 billion/year system-cost figure is an **external citation** (Adrion et al. 2015, an insurance-claims study of >50,000 Lyme patients), not a MyLymeData-generated estimate, and no price year is stated in the chartbook.

## Limitations
**Claims undercounting:** The $1B figure is based on insurance claims. The chartbook itself reports that roughly half of PLD patients' treating providers do not accept insurance, so care from non-network providers would not appear in that claims-based figure - it likely undercounts the true healthcare system cost of Lyme disease.

**Subgroup disaggregation:** The utilization figures (doctor visits, ER visits, hospital stays, home care visits) are reported as single pooled national numbers with no breakdown by sex, age, race/ethnicity, disability, or other subgroup. The document does not state whether these rates vary by subgroup. Federal survey data (MEPS, NHIS, BRFSS) generally supports this kind of disaggregated analysis even though this document did not perform it.

**Systemic gap:** The chartbook states that despite a growing number of persistent Lyme disease cases, very little research has been conducted on how best to treat them, and separately describes most PLD-treating clinicians as operating outside insurance and Medicare/Medicaid networks, facing prior-authorization burdens and professional stigma - a combined clinician-training and research-pipeline gap distinct from the cost-accuracy and funding points above.

**Sex/gender:** A 2023 MyLymeData sub-study (not modeled as a separate input here) found women reported more co-infections, longer diagnostic delays, greater symptom severity, and more frequent misdiagnosis with chronic fatigue syndrome, fibromyalgia, or psychiatric disorders than men; no sex difference was found in treatment response or side effects. This pooled chartbook does not disaggregate the modeled inputs above by sex.

## Boundaries
This is a self-selected patient registry, not a nationally representative sample; percentages describe this sample only. No MyLymeData-generated dollar cost exists for comparison to the external $1B figure.

outputs.interpretation: A higher value means more patients were told they had a different condition before Lyme disease was identified. At the document's reported value of 74%, misdiagnosis before correct diagnosis was common in this sample; this is a distinct measure from the time-based late-diagnosis figure above, since a patient can be both quickly AND incorrectly diagnosed, or slowly and correctly diagnosed.

outputs.label: Share of PLD patients whose treating provider does not accept insurance
outputs.interpretation: A higher value means more patients had to see a clinician operating outside insurance networks to get treatment. At the document's reported value of 50%, about half of this sample faced this barrier, which the chartbook links to broader clinician-level insurance non-participation (also reported at page 19).

outputs.label: PLD minus general-population annual doctor visits (positive = PLD patients report more visits per year than the general-population comparator)
outputs.interpretation: A larger positive value means persistent Lyme disease patients in this sample report visiting doctors far more often per year than the general-population comparator. At the document's reported defaults (19.4 vs. 1.09), this gap is about 18 additional visits per year, consistent with the chartbook's framing of persistent Lyme disease as a high-utilization condition; both figures are self-reported, not claims-derived.

outputs.label: Externally cited annual U.S. healthcare system cost attributable to Lyme disease (insurance claims, price year not stated)
outputs.interpretation: This reproduces the single external estimate the chartbook cites (Adrion et al. 2015) rather than any figure MyLymeData itself computed. Because it is based on insurance claims, and the same document reports that roughly half of PLD patients' providers do not accept insurance, this number likely undercounts the true system cost of Lyme disease care.

scenarios.label: Mostly out-of-network care
scenarios.goal: Shows how true system cost could differ if most providers were out-of-network.
scenarios.description: Raises the share of providers not accepting insurance to an illustrative 90% and the claims-based system-cost figure to its assumed upper bound of $2B, reflecting the chartbook's own caveat that claims data miss out-of-network care.

scenarios.label: Mostly in-network care
scenarios.goal: Shows how access barriers would look if nearly all providers accepted insurance.
scenarios.description: Lowers the share of providers not accepting insurance from the observed 50% to an illustrative assumed 10%, showing the opposite extreme of the access-barrier output.

scenarios.label: Lower-delay case mix
scenarios.goal: Illustrates diagnosis outputs under a less-delayed, less-misdiagnosed case mix, not an intervention.
scenarios.description: Lowers the late-diagnosis and misdiagnosis shares from the observed 77% and 74% to an illustrative 30% each, showing the resulting outputs under a different hypothetical case mix with no causal claim, since the source data are observational.

scenarios.label: Narrower utilization gap
scenarios.goal: Tests how small the utilization gap could be if general-population visits were higher.
scenarios.description: Raises the general-population comparator from the reported 1.09 visits/year to the input's assumed illustrative maximum of 3, narrowing the computed utilization-gap output accordingly.

scenarios.label: Wider utilization gap
scenarios.goal: Tests how large the utilization gap could be with higher PLD visit rates.
scenarios.description: Raises PLD patients' annual doctor-visit rate from the observed mean of 19.4 to the input's assumed illustrative maximum of 40, widening the computed utilization-gap output accordingly.

trajectories.label: Cumulative excess doctor visits per PLD patient (flat, assumes the reported annual gap repeats unchanged each year - not a growth projection)
trajectories.unit: visits (cumulative, per PLD patient, vs. general-population comparator)
